gold_insights.insight: This section contains no references to EU regulations (e.g., DSA, GDPR, AI Act, Data Act) and does not describe mechanisms for researcher access to algorithms or public data; beyond releasing the model on Hugging Face, no DSA-style transparency or compliance dialogue features are specified.

The authors explicitly state that post-training should not attempt to impart novel cybersecurity knowledge and that they rely primarily on pre-training of the base model for domain knowledge (Section 5.1), implying no targeted inclusion of EU regulatory corpora during instruction-tuning.

Although security evaluations include coverage of security governance and compliance (Section 3.1), no EU-specific compliance benchmarks are listed (Table 1), and topic coverage across benchmarks is skewed—application security is overrepresented while cloud security and security operations are underrepresented (Figure 2)—which risks blind spots for enterprise compliance use cases (e.g., IoT contexts that depend on cloud and operational security).

The model shows strong instruction-following but the authors note that MMLU hints at a narrow base of knowledge and BigBenchHard suggests potential for further development in reasoning capabilities (Section 6.3), indicating potential limitations for complex, multi-regime compliance reasoning (e.g., simultaneously addressing GDPR, Data Act, and AI Act).

Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct has not undergone dedicated safety alignment procedures beyond basic instruction-tuning; it is not explicitly trained for robustness against adversarial techniques (e.g., jailbreaking or prompt injection), no post-hoc safety filtering has been applied to its outputs, and the authors strongly recommend adding additional safety layers (e.g., automated content filtering or LLM-based moderation) when deploying or experimenting with this model.

In HarmBench safety testing (400 representative prompts for simple toxicity), Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct rejected or safely responded to 92% of malicious examples; when paired with LlamaGuard’s taxonomy-driven input-output filtering, the combined system rejected 99% of malicious test cases, and the authors recommend deploying the model with additional guardrails in production use cases.

A detailed system prompt is baked into the model’s chat template, was found in internal testing to improve user satisfaction and safety, and can be modified or overridden and tailored to particular use cases.

This section presents no claims of explicit alignment to EU regulatory transparency or compliance requirements (e.g., DSA, AI Act); the focus is on general-purpose cybersecurity dialogue, persona adaptation, and baseline safety, with GDPR only cited in the references and without corresponding compliance training or alignment procedures described.
CTIBench-MCQA draws from CTI frameworks, regulations, and taxonomies such as NIST, GDPR, MITRE ATT&CK, and CAPEC, indicating explicit coverage of GDPR-derived questions in the model’s evaluation.

The Cybersecurity Taxonomy explicitly includes Governance, Risk, and Compliance (GRC) with ‘Compliance and Regulations (e.g., GDPR, HIPAA)’, as well as ‘IoT and OT/ICS Security’ and ‘Cloud Compliance & Shared Responsibility Model’, aligning the intended scope with IoT-centric and regulatory compliance topics.

General capability benchmarks include IFEval, which tests verifiable instruction-following (25 instruction types, ~500 prompts) and is used to assess downstream usability in cybersecurity workflows, and AlpacaEval 2 to measure chat alignment, supporting structured, compliance-ready responses.

This section explicitly references GDPR but does not mention the EU DSA, AI Act, or Data Act in the listed benchmarks or taxonomy; additionally, the post-training data analysis relied on an English-only keyword bank and filtered out non-English prompts using a FastText language detection model, indicating an English-centric focus that may omit member-state-localized requirements.

The recommended system prompt enforces transparency and precision in responses: it instructs to "Always try to cite sources when you are using an important piece of information in your response," to "Think step-by-step before producing a response," and requires CTI and cloud outputs to be exact (e.g., CTI identifiers must be "absolutely correct"; for cloud security, "Make sure these are absolutely correct... Cite sources... and explain your logic thoroughly").

The model’s scope is explicitly limited to cybersecurity, with a refusal policy for out-of-scope topics: "If the user asks questions not directly related to cybersecurity, you must also politely refuse the query and explain that you are only knowledgeable in cybersecurity," and it must refuse harmful or unsafe requests ("especially pertaining to generating malware or ransomware").

PersonaGym is used to assess dialogue alignment, including explainability and safety aspects: evaluation spans five dimensions—"Action Justification," "Expected Action," "Linguistic Habits," "Persona Consistency," and "Toxicity Control"—and the model was evaluated on a subset of 50 personas from the test split.

The data decontamination process uses high similarity thresholds and human-in-the-loop checks: candidates are retained only with cosine similarity ≥ 0.8 (with a 0.95 upper bound), and a subset of high-similarity matches is validated via an "LLM-as-a-judge" to reduce false positives; the report notes that "decontamination cannot fully eliminate contamination" but it "significantly reduces the risk of benchmark leakage and improves the reliability of downstream evaluation."
